title: Zakat, done
tomorrow: a credit card offer with your name in gold. now what?

cards: A plate passed down a church pew on a Sunday morning, envelopes dropping in. And across town, at a kitchen table, a calculator, a pen, and a worksheet with one word across the top: zakat. Both are giving.
Both are worship. So one question for today: what does it mean for giving to be done?

teach.b: Zakat is one of the pillars the Prophet ﷺ said Islam is built on. It isn't whatever you feel like giving; that's sadaqah, voluntary charity, and it's welcome any day. Zakat has rules.
Wealth above a threshold, the nisab, held for a year. A share of it: in Abu Bakr's letter preserved in Sahih al-Bukhari, a quarter of a tenth on silver.

And the people it goes to are named in the Qur'an itself, the poor, the needy, the debtor, the traveler and more, and called, in Pickthall's words, "a duty imposed by Allah." So zakat ends like a bill ends.
Worked out, handed over, paid. Christians know giving as worship too.
In the King James Bible, Paul writes: "Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
What's shared is real: giving as part of faith, done gladly, for God and not for show. And an honest difference.

teach.h: THE HEART DECIDES, OR THE RULE DOES.
teach.b: Paul's line leaves the amount to each person's heart.
Zakat sets the share and the recipients by design. Islam keeps both kinds of giving: the fixed duty, and sadaqah, as the heart decides.

how: Muslims whose wealth passes the nisab threshold for a year work out their zakat, often with a worksheet, an online calculator or a local imam's help, and pay it to eligible recipients; some choose to pay it in Ramadan.

o: a set share of wealth given yearly as a duty to those in need
any voluntary gift given whenever the heart is moved
a fee paid to the masjid for its upkeep each year

games.q: two kinds of giving, and a neighbor — tap the pairs.
p: a set share, paid once due
whom God loves, in Paul's letter

s: zakat is whatever amount you choose to give
that's sadaqah. zakat has a threshold, a set share and named recipients.
the Qur'an itself names who zakat is for
9:60 names them, and calls it a duty imposed by Allah.
Paul writes that God loves a cheerful giver
2 Corinthians 9:7, in the King James Bible.

games.q: Dadi's worksheet shows zakat is due, but she's already given a lot of voluntary charity this year. does that count as her zakat?
o: yes; all charity counts toward zakat, whatever it was meant as.
zakat is its own duty; the voluntary giving was sadaqah, on top.
she can skip it, since she's already given more than the share.
games.why: zakat and sadaqah are two kinds of giving. the duty is worked out and paid as zakat; the voluntary gifts stand on their own.

practice: On paper or in your head, list what you hold: cash, savings, any gold or silver, things kept to sell. Next to the list, name who a share would go to, from the people the Qur'an names.
If zakat isn't yours to pay, list one gift you'd give gladly instead, and to whom.

wordCard.voice: Zakat: the set yearly share of wealth above a threshold, paid as a duty to the people the Qur'an names. One of the pillars.

orig.note: Arabic: the obligatory alms, one of the pillars of Islam.

carryVoice: Your line: paid. Not a mood, a duty worked out and handed over. Six of ten.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 8 (Islam is built on five, including paying zakat)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1454 (Abu Bakr's letter on zakat: on silver, a quarter of a tenth)
Sunan Abi Dawud 1573 (no zakat on wealth until a year has passed over it)
